hints: Start by thinking about what normally stops a healthy body cell from dividing all the time - what control system must be broken?
Link that broken control to what happens to mitosis and cell survival, and what a growing pile of identical abnormal cells is called.
walkthrough:
Remember Normal Cell Cycle Control**
Healthy body cells only divide when needed because genes such as proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes switch division on and off at checkpoints. Think of them as accelerators and brakes.

Link Mutation to Loss of Control**
A mutation can damage those genes, so the cell cycle is no longer regulated and apoptosis does not occur. The cell becomes effectively immortal and divides by uncontrolled mitosis, building up a mass of abnormal cells - the tumour.

Final answer: Mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle lead to uncontrolled mitosis / cell division and failure of programmed cell death (apoptosis), producing a mass of abnormal cells forming a tumour.

hints: Focus on the smallest possible change in DNA that could still alter a protein - what happens if just one base in the sequence is swapped?
Follow that change through transcription and translation - how does an altered triplet and codon change which tRNA can bind?
walkthrough:
From One Base to One Codon**
A point substitution changes a single nucleotide in DNA. That changes one triplet, so after transcription the mRNA has one changed codon. Only one codon is affected, which fits the one amino acid difference.

From Codon to Altered Protein**
At translation, the new codon pairs with a different tRNA anticodon carrying a different amino acid. The primary structure is therefore changed by one amino acid, which alters folding and tertiary structure to give the tumour specific antigen.

Final answer: Substitution of a single nucleotide / base changes one DNA triplet and hence one mRNA codon, so a tRNA with a different anticodon brings a different amino acid, altering the primary and tertiary structure of the surface protein to form TSA.

hints: Think of the vaccine TSA as a practice target - which cells first pick up foreign antigen and show it to lymphocytes?
Recall how the immune system picks the correct lymphocyte for one specific antigen and then makes many copies of it.
Now connect those activated killer cells to real tumour cells in the body - how do they recognise and destroy a cell carrying the same TSA?
walkthrough:
Presentation and Specific Recognition**
The vaccine TSA acts as antigen. It is engulfed by a phagocyte and presented to T-lymphocytes. Only a T-lymphocyte with a complementary specific receptor will bind the TSA. This is clonal selection - one cell type selected by one shape.

Clonal Expansion to Build an Army**
That selected cytotoxic T cell (killer T cell) divides rapidly by mitosis to form a clone. Vaccination therefore builds a large population ready to recognise the same TSA without needing a first slow infection.

Killing Tumour Cells**
When these cytotoxic T cells meet a tumour cell displaying the same TSA on its surface, their receptors bind to it. They release perforin and other toxins such as hydrogen peroxide or granzymes, which cause lysis and death of the tumour cell.

Final answer: Vaccination with TSA stimulates a specific immune response. TSA is presented to T-lymphocytes and binds to a complementary receptor on a specific cytotoxic T cell, triggering clonal expansion by mitosis. Cytotoxic T cells then bind to TSA on tumour cells and release perforin / lytic enzymes to kill them.

hints: Compare one single lab-made TSA with a whole tumour cell taken from the patient - which one is guaranteed to match all the antigens on that person's cancer?
Now think about the practical and biological price of that personal match - what about surgery, time, cost, and the risk the immune system still sees the cells as self?
walkthrough:
Why Whole Patient Cells Can Work Better**
A single TSA vaccine only protects against one antigen, but a tumour may have several different TSAs. Using the patient's own tumour cells means the vaccine contains the appropriate antigens exactly as they appear on that tumour, so multiple specific clones of T cells are stimulated. It is personalised and more likely to be effective.

Why It Can Be Difficult or Fail**
That personal match has costs. Enough cells must be removed by surgery, which is invasive and may not be possible if the tumour is small, and making an individual vaccine is expensive and slow. Biologically, the immune system may still tolerate the cells as self and not respond, or tumour cells in the body may not all carry the same antigens, so some escape destruction.

Final answer: Advantage: patient's own tumour cells carry the exact set of TSAs present on the tumour, including multiple TSAs, so a specific immune response to each is stimulated and treatment is personalised and more effective. Disadvantage: requires surgery to remove enough tumour cells and is high cost / time-consuming; or tumour cells may not be recognised as foreign / non-self, or may lack the TSA, so response fails.
